lessons.title: Public Transport vs New Roads
lessons.question: Governments should spend more money on public transport than on building new roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
lessons.thesis: I largely agree: reliable public transport uses limited urban space more efficiently and offers a more sustainable long-term response to congestion, although some road investment remains necessary.
lessons.memory: Move more people, not simply more cars
plan: R1: Mass transit moves far more people through limited urban space.
Mechanism: reliable services make leaving the car at home realistic.
R2/concession: roads still need maintenance and selective expansion.
Evaluation: priority should go to capacity and long-term mobility, not road building alone.
essay: Governments must decide how transport budgets should be divided between public transport and new roads. I largely agree that a greater share should go to buses, rail and mass transit. These systems can move large numbers of people through limited urban space and provide a more sustainable response to congestion, although some road investment will always be necessary.

The strongest argument for prioritising public transport is its ability to increase the capacity of an existing transport network without requiring every traveller to use a separate vehicle. A frequent metro line or dedicated bus corridor can carry thousands of commuters during peak periods, whereas the same number of people in private cars would occupy far more road space. If services are reliable, affordable and well connected, some drivers will choose not to use their cars for routine journeys. This can reduce congestion while also improving access for people who cannot drive, including teenagers, older residents and lower-income workers.

New roads, by contrast, are not a complete solution to urban traffic. Additional lanes may relieve a particular bottleneck temporarily, but they can also encourage more driving and shift congestion to another part of the network. Nevertheless, roads remain essential for freight, emergency services and areas that cannot be served efficiently by rail. Governments should therefore maintain existing roads and build new links where there is a clear need, while directing the larger share of new investment towards high-capacity public transport. This balanced approach recognises that different journeys require different infrastructure.

In conclusion, I agree that public transport should receive more government funding than new road construction. Roads remain necessary, but mass transit generally provides greater capacity, broader access and a more durable way to manage travel demand in growing cities.

lessons.title: Banning Private Cars from City Centres
lessons.question: Private cars should be banned from city centres in order to reduce traffic congestion and air pollution. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
lessons.thesis: I partly agree: restricting private cars in the busiest central areas can reduce congestion and pollution, but a complete ban is too inflexible unless strong alternatives and exemptions are available.
lessons.memory: Restrict where pressure is highest; preserve essential access
plan: R1: Fewer private cars can free road space and reduce local emissions.
Example: pedestrian/transit zones in dense commercial centres.
R2: a total ban can disadvantage disabled people, trades and poorly served commuters.
Evaluation: targeted restrictions + exemptions + strong alternatives are more proportionate.
essay: Banning private cars from city centres is often proposed as a way to tackle congestion and air pollution. I partly agree with this approach. Restricting car access in the busiest central districts can make streets cleaner and more efficient, but a complete ban would be too inflexible unless cities first provide reliable alternatives and sensible exemptions.

There is a strong case for reducing the number of private vehicles in dense urban centres. Road space in these areas is limited, yet a car often carries only one or two people. Replacing some car journeys with buses, trains, walking or cycling can therefore allow the same streets to move more people. Fewer vehicles also mean less exhaust pollution at street level, which is particularly valuable in places where many pedestrians live, work or shop. For example, a central shopping district with good rail connections could reserve several streets for buses, deliveries at set times and pedestrians, making short journeys faster and the public space more pleasant.

A blanket ban, however, could create unfair or impractical consequences. Some disabled people depend on private vehicles, while tradespeople may need to carry equipment that cannot easily be taken on public transport. Residents travelling from poorly connected suburbs may also have no realistic alternative. For this reason, cities should use targeted measures such as low-traffic zones, congestion charges and limited permits rather than prohibit every private car. Restrictions should be introduced alongside frequent public transport and park-and-ride facilities so that changing travel behaviour is feasible rather than simply punitive.

In conclusion, I support substantial restrictions on private cars in congested city centres, but not an absolute ban. A targeted system can reduce traffic and pollution while preserving access for journeys that genuinely require a private vehicle.

lessons.title: Higher Fuel Prices vs Better Public Transport
lessons.question: Some people believe that increasing the price of fuel is the best way to reduce traffic congestion and pollution, while others think that improving public transport is more effective. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
lessons.thesis: Both approaches can influence travel behaviour, but I favour improving public transport because it gives people a practical alternative rather than relying mainly on financial pressure.
lessons.memory: Price can discourage; alternatives enable change
plan: View A: higher fuel prices make unnecessary driving more expensive.
Limit: burden falls unevenly where alternatives are weak.
View B: better public transport changes the practical choice available.
Opinion: improve alternatives first; pricing can play a supporting role.
essay: There is debate over whether higher fuel prices or better public transport would be more effective in reducing congestion and pollution. Raising the cost of driving can discourage car use, while improved services can make alternatives more attractive. Both approaches have merit, but I believe public transport should be the main strategy because it enables people to change behaviour rather than simply making existing journeys more expensive.

Supporters of higher fuel prices argue that drivers respond to financial incentives. If each car journey costs more, people may combine trips, share vehicles or use public transport when a car is unnecessary. Higher prices can also encourage more fuel-efficient vehicles. This approach can affect travel quickly without waiting for major infrastructure projects. However, its impact is uneven. A worker with no reliable bus or rail service may have little choice but to keep driving, so the policy can raise household costs without reducing traffic substantially.

Those who favour better public transport focus on expanding travellers’ choices. Frequent buses, integrated fares and reliable rail make it possible for commuters to leave cars at home without sacrificing excessive time or convenience. In my view, this is stronger in the long term because behaviour is more likely to change when an acceptable substitute exists. For example, a commuter may switch to a train if it is punctual and connects conveniently with local buses. Fuel taxes can still play a supporting role, but they are fairer when realistic alternatives already exist.

In conclusion, higher fuel prices can discourage some car use, but improved public transport addresses the problem more constructively by making lower-pollution travel practical. I would therefore prioritise service quality and coverage, using fuel pricing only as a complementary measure.

lessons.title: Railways vs Roads
lessons.question: Some people believe that governments should prioritise investment in railways, while others think that roads are more important. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
lessons.thesis: Rail and road networks serve different functions, but I favour giving new investment priority to rail in densely populated corridors while maintaining roads for local access, freight and emergency services.
lessons.memory: Rail for high-volume corridors; roads for flexible access
plan: View A: rail moves many people efficiently between dense centres.
View B: roads provide flexible door-to-door access and carry freight.
Evaluation criterion: population density and journey type.
Opinion: prioritise rail where demand is concentrated, maintain roads everywhere.
essay: Transport budgets often force governments to choose between investment in railways and roads. Supporters of rail emphasise capacity and efficiency, whereas advocates of roads value flexibility and wide geographic coverage. In my view, both are essential, but new investment should generally favour rail on busy urban and intercity corridors, while roads should continue to receive sufficient funding for maintenance and essential access.

Those who prioritise railways argue that trains can move large numbers of passengers using relatively little land. In densely populated areas, a frequent rail service can connect homes, employment centres and regional cities without adding thousands of cars to already crowded roads. Rail can also provide predictable journey times because trains are not normally delayed by road congestion. These advantages are important where demand is concentrated along a clear corridor. A well-used commuter line, for example, can reduce pressure on parallel highways and give travellers a reliable alternative during peak periods.

Supporters of roads, however, point out that road transport is more flexible. Trucks deliver goods directly to shops and factories, buses serve routes that would not justify a railway, and emergency vehicles need a road network. Rural communities also depend on roads because homes and businesses are widely dispersed. I agree that these functions make road maintenance indispensable. Nevertheless, constructing ever more lanes in dense cities is often less efficient than increasing rail capacity. The sensible priority therefore depends on location: rail deserves greater investment where passenger demand is high, while roads remain the backbone of local and freight access.

In conclusion, roads and railways should not be treated as substitutes in every situation. I would prioritise rail investment on heavily travelled corridors, but maintain a strong road network for flexible local movement, freight and essential services.

lessons.title: Growth of Ride-Hailing Apps
lessons.question: An increasing number of people use ride-hailing apps instead of traditional taxis or public transport. Is this a positive or negative development?
lessons.thesis: I regard the growth of ride-hailing as mixed but negative overall when it replaces high-capacity public transport, because convenience for individual users can increase vehicle traffic and weaken shared transport.

essay: Ride-hailing applications have changed urban travel by allowing passengers to request a car within minutes. Although these services offer genuine convenience, I regard their growing use as a negative development overall when they replace public transport. The main reason is that individual convenience can come at the cost of more vehicles on crowded streets and weaker demand for high-capacity services.

Ride-hailing is useful in situations where conventional transport performs poorly. Passengers can book a journey late at night, travel directly with luggage or complete the final part of a trip from a railway station to a neighbourhood with limited bus service. App-based payment and route tracking may also make the service easier to use than an unfamiliar local taxi system. In these roles, ride-hailing can complement public transport rather than compete with it, especially for travellers who cannot easily walk or cycle.

The problem arises when large numbers of commuters choose a private ride instead of a bus or train. A car carrying one passenger occupies far more road space per person than mass transit, and drivers may travel empty while waiting for the next customer. This can add traffic even if the service is shared through an app. Falling public-transport demand can also make frequent services harder to justify financially. Cities should therefore encourage ride-hailing as a first- or last-mile option while keeping buses and rail attractive for high-volume journeys.

In conclusion, ride-hailing has valuable uses, but its expansion is negative if it routinely replaces public transport. Its strongest role is to fill gaps in a shared transport network, not to become the default mode for everyday commuting.

lessons.title: Bicycle-Sharing and E-Scooter Schemes
lessons.question: More cities are introducing bicycle-sharing and electric scooter schemes for short urban journeys. Is this a positive or negative development?
lessons.thesis: I consider this a positive development overall because shared micromobility can replace short car trips and improve access to public transport, provided that cities manage safety and parking properly.

Judgement: positive if infrastructure and rules are designed with the service.
essay: Shared bicycles and electric scooters are becoming common in many cities as an option for short journeys. I consider this a positive development overall because these small vehicles can replace some car trips and connect people more easily to public transport. Their benefits, however, depend on safe infrastructure and effective rules for parking and riding.

The main advantage is that micromobility suits journeys that are too far to walk but too short to justify a car. A resident might cycle two kilometres to a railway station instead of driving and searching for parking. When many people make similar choices, road space is used more efficiently and local emissions can fall. Shared schemes also allow occasional users to travel without owning a bicycle or scooter, which makes the option available to visitors and people who have limited storage space at home.

Nevertheless, rapid expansion can create safety and accessibility problems. Scooters left across pavements can obstruct wheelchair users and pedestrians, while riders may be injured if they are forced to mix with fast traffic. These drawbacks are not reasons to reject the idea, but they require deliberate management. Cities can provide protected lanes, marked parking areas and lower speed limits in crowded zones. Operators can also use app-based parking controls and maintain vehicles regularly. With these measures, the service can support rather than disrupt the wider transport system.

In conclusion, bicycle-sharing and e-scooter schemes are a positive addition to urban transport when they are integrated with public transit and safe street design. Good regulation is essential, but the potential to replace short car trips makes the development worthwhile.

lessons.title: Building Metro Systems
lessons.question: Many large cities are building or expanding metro and underground railway systems. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this development?
lessons.thesis: Metro systems can provide high-capacity, reliable urban transport and support compact development, but they require enormous upfront investment and can cause years of construction disruption.

essay: Many large cities are investing in metro or underground railway systems to cope with growing travel demand. Such networks can move large numbers of passengers reliably and can support more compact urban development. Their main disadvantages are the enormous initial cost and the disruption created during construction. Whether a metro represents good value therefore depends heavily on local demand and planning quality.

One important advantage is capacity. Trains operating on their own tracks can carry thousands of passengers without being delayed by road traffic, making journey times more predictable during peak periods. Stations can also become focal points for housing, offices and shops, allowing more people to live within walking distance of high-quality transport. This can reduce dependence on private cars and make dense city centres easier to reach. Once a network is well connected, passengers can transfer between lines and complete many daily journeys without needing a vehicle.

The disadvantages are mainly financial and practical. Underground construction requires expensive engineering, land acquisition and safety systems, and projects may take many years before passengers receive any benefit. During that period, road closures, noise and excavation can disrupt businesses and residents. There is also a risk of poor value if a line is built where passenger demand is too low. Governments must therefore compare metro investment with alternatives such as bus rapid transit, which may offer adequate capacity at lower cost in less dense areas.

In conclusion, metro systems offer major advantages in crowded cities through high capacity and reliable travel, but they are costly and disruptive to build. They are most suitable where long-term passenger demand is strong enough to justify the investment.

lessons.title: Remote Work and Commuting
lessons.question: Some employers encourage staff to work from home in order to reduce commuting. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this development for transport and city life?
lessons.thesis: Working from home can reduce peak-hour travel and give cities more flexible use of road and transit capacity, but widespread remote work can weaken public-transport revenue and reduce activity in business districts.
lessons.memory: Less commuting changes both traffic and the city around it

Disadvantage: lower ridership can weaken transit finances; business districts lose footfall.

essay: Encouraging employees to work from home can change not only working habits but also the way cities move. The main advantage is a reduction in peak-hour commuting, which can ease pressure on roads and public transport. However, if remote work becomes widespread, lower passenger numbers may weaken transport revenue and central business districts may lose some of the daily activity that supports shops and services.

Fewer commuters can make transport networks operate more smoothly at their busiest times. When some employees stay home, trains are less crowded and roads may experience fewer severe bottlenecks, even if total travel does not disappear. Workers also save the time and cost of travelling to an office, while cities may benefit from lower emissions during peak periods. A hybrid schedule can be particularly useful because different employees travel on different days, spreading demand across the week rather than concentrating every journey into the same morning and evening periods.

There are, nevertheless, wider disadvantages. Public transport systems have high fixed costs, so a sustained fall in fare-paying passengers can make frequent services harder to finance. Cutting services in response may then harm people who cannot work remotely and still depend on buses or trains. Business districts can also lose customers when fewer office workers buy meals, use local services or shop nearby. These effects do not mean remote work should be discouraged, but transport agencies and city centres may need to adapt their funding and land use to new travel patterns.

lessons.title: Congestion Charging
lessons.question: More cities are charging drivers a fee to enter congested central areas. Do the advantages of this policy outweigh the disadvantages?
lessons.thesis: I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages when charges are paired with good alternatives, because reduced congestion and more reliable travel benefit a large number of users, while the main equity concerns can be mitigated through design.

essay: Congestion charging requires drivers to pay for entering the busiest parts of a city, usually at times when road space is under greatest pressure. The policy can impose additional costs on some households and businesses, but I believe its advantages outweigh these disadvantages when the revenue is used to improve alternatives and vulnerable users receive appropriate protection.

The main drawback is fairness. A flat charge represents a larger share of income for a low-paid worker than for a wealthy driver, and some people travel by car because their working hours or location are poorly served by public transport. Small firms that make deliveries may also face higher operating costs. These concerns are significant, but they can be reduced through discounts for low-income residents, exemptions for essential vehicles and better park-and-ride or public transport services. The disadvantage is therefore partly a question of policy design rather than an unavoidable feature of charging.

The benefits can affect a much wider group. When some drivers change route, time or mode, traffic becomes more manageable and buses can operate more reliably because they spend less time in queues. Pedestrians and cyclists may also experience quieter streets and lower local emissions. Importantly, the charge creates a source of revenue that can be reinvested in transport improvements, allowing the policy to strengthen the alternatives that drivers need. These network-wide and continuing gains carry greater weight than costs that can be targeted through exemptions and support.

In conclusion, congestion charging has genuine distributional disadvantages, but its advantages are greater when the scheme is carefully designed. Reduced traffic, more reliable transport and reinvestment in alternatives can produce lasting benefits for the city as a whole.

lessons.title: High-Speed Rail vs Short-Haul Flights
lessons.question: High-speed rail is replacing short-haul domestic flights between some major cities. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
lessons.thesis: I believe the advantages generally outweigh the disadvantages on busy medium-distance routes because rail can provide city-centre access with lower transport emissions, while its high infrastructure cost is justified only where demand is consistently strong.
lessons.memory: Use rail where distance and demand make it efficient
plan: Weaker side: rail infrastructure is expensive and geographically inflexible.
Stronger side: city-centre links, high capacity and lower operational emissions.
Comparison: long-lived network benefits vs upfront cost.
Condition: busy medium-distance corridors, not every route.
essay: High-speed rail is increasingly competing with short domestic flights between major cities. Building such railways is expensive and not suitable for every route, yet I believe the advantages generally outweigh the disadvantages where passenger demand is high and distances are moderate. In these circumstances, rail can provide convenient city-centre travel while reducing the environmental cost of frequent short flights.

The strongest disadvantage is the scale of the initial investment. High-speed lines require specialised track, stations, land and long construction periods, so a poorly chosen route can leave the public with a costly asset that attracts too few passengers. Rail is also less flexible than aviation because tracks cannot easily be redirected when travel patterns change. For very long distances or routes crossing difficult terrain, flying may remain more practical. These limitations mean that replacing flights with rail should be selective rather than a universal policy.

On suitable corridors, however, the benefits are substantial and long lasting. Trains can carry many passengers and usually connect central stations, reducing the extra time needed to travel to distant airports and pass through security procedures. Electric rail can also produce lower operational emissions per passenger, particularly where the electricity supply is relatively clean. Once built, a busy line can serve travellers for decades and release airport capacity for routes where aviation has a clearer advantage. These continuing benefits can justify the high upfront cost when ridership is strong.

In conclusion, high-speed rail should not replace every domestic flight, but its advantages outweigh the disadvantages on busy medium-distance routes. The key is to invest where demand, geography and journey time allow rail to perform efficiently.

lessons.title: Dependence on Private Cars
lessons.question: Many cities are heavily dependent on private cars. What problems can this cause, and what measures can governments take to address them?
lessons.thesis: Car dependence can produce chronic congestion, unequal access and inefficient use of urban space; governments should respond by improving alternatives and managing car use rather than relying on road expansion alone.
lessons.memory: Car dependence is a system problem, so the solution must change the system
plan: Problem 1: congestion and space consumed by moving/parking cars.
Problem 2: people without cars face weaker access to jobs/services.
Solution: reliable public transport + safe walking/cycling networks.
Management: parking/congestion policies make alternatives competitive.
essay: Heavy dependence on private cars creates more than slow traffic. It can produce persistent congestion, consume large amounts of urban space and disadvantage people who cannot afford or operate a vehicle. Governments can address these problems by making alternatives genuinely practical and by managing car use in the places where road space is most limited.

One major problem is that a car-dependent city requires enormous space for roads and parking. As the number of vehicles rises, bottlenecks become common and governments may respond by widening roads, which can remove land from housing, footpaths or public space. Dependence on cars also creates an access problem. A household without a vehicle may find it difficult to reach employment, education or healthcare if buses are infrequent and destinations are widely separated. Transport inequality therefore becomes linked to income, age and physical ability rather than simply personal preference.

To address these problems, governments should first build a connected network of reliable buses or rail services and safe walking and cycling routes. Frequent services are crucial because an alternative that requires long waits will not persuade many drivers to change. Land-use planning can also place new housing and services near transport corridors. In the busiest areas, parking charges or congestion fees can discourage unnecessary driving, with revenue reinvested in public transport. These measures work together: better alternatives expand choice, while pricing prevents scarce road space from being treated as unlimited.

In conclusion, car dependence can worsen congestion, waste urban land and restrict access for non-drivers. A combination of high-quality alternatives, better planning and targeted demand management can reduce these problems more effectively than continuous road expansion.

essay: Rural public transport is often difficult to provide because passengers are spread across large areas, yet limited services can create serious social and economic problems. People who do not drive may become isolated from jobs, education and healthcare, while households can be forced to bear the cost of owning a car. Solutions should therefore be flexible enough to match lower population density rather than simply copying urban bus networks.

The most serious problem is restricted access. An older resident may be unable to attend a medical appointment if the only bus leaves early in the morning and returns before the appointment ends. Young people can face similar barriers when travelling to college or part-time work. Limited transport can also reduce employment options for adults, because accepting a job in another town may be impossible without a vehicle. Over time, this can encourage younger residents to leave and can make rural communities less attractive to businesses and essential service providers.

To address this problem, authorities can combine several forms of transport. Demand-responsive minibuses can adjust routes according to bookings, while community transport can serve passengers who need additional assistance. Because low-density routes may never cover their costs through fares alone, targeted public subsidies are often necessary to maintain a basic level of service. Timetables should also connect local vehicles with regional rail or bus hubs, allowing one rural service to provide access to a much larger network. Digital booking can help, but telephone options should remain for passengers who are less comfortable online.

In conclusion, infrequent rural transport can restrict opportunity and deepen isolation. Flexible local services, appropriate subsidies and well-planned connections can provide essential mobility without requiring rural areas to operate the same high-frequency systems as cities.

lessons.title: Why Congestion Keeps Worsening
lessons.question: Traffic congestion continues to worsen in many cities despite the construction of new roads. What are the main reasons for this, and what measures could reduce congestion?
lessons.thesis: Congestion persists because road expansion can stimulate additional driving while jobs and services remain concentrated; reducing it requires attractive alternatives, better land-use planning and targeted management of peak demand.
lessons.memory: More road capacity can create more traffic if demand keeps growing
plan: Cause 1: new capacity lowers the short-term cost of driving and attracts more trips.
Cause 2: dispersed housing + concentrated jobs create long car commutes.
Solution: high-quality alternatives and transit-oriented development.
Demand measure: parking/congestion pricing and flexible work times.
essay: Many cities continue to experience worsening congestion even after constructing new roads. This happens partly because extra road capacity can encourage additional car use and partly because urban development often creates long journeys between homes, jobs and services. Reducing congestion therefore requires policies that influence travel demand as well as investment in alternatives to driving.

One important cause is that road expansion can make driving temporarily faster, encouraging people to make trips they previously avoided, travel at busier times or move farther from their workplace. As traffic grows, the new capacity gradually fills and congestion returns. A second cause is land-use pattern. When affordable housing is located far from major employment areas and public transport is weak, large numbers of commuters have little practical choice but to drive. Building another road may move the bottleneck, but it does not remove the underlying need for long car journeys.

Governments can respond by improving reliable public transport on busy corridors and by planning new housing, schools and services around those networks. This gives residents realistic alternatives and can shorten some daily journeys. In the most congested areas, parking charges or road-use fees can discourage unnecessary peak-hour driving, especially if the revenue is reinvested in buses and rail. Employers can also support flexible start times, which spreads demand beyond a narrow rush-hour period. Together, these measures address both the amount and timing of traffic.

In conclusion, congestion often survives road building because travel demand expands and urban form continues to generate car-dependent journeys. Better alternatives, coordinated land use and targeted demand management are more likely to produce lasting improvement than road construction alone.

lessons.title: Decline in Walking and Cycling
lessons.question: In many cities, fewer people walk or cycle for their daily journeys. What are the main causes of this trend, and what measures could encourage more active travel?
lessons.thesis: Active travel declines when destinations are too far apart and streets feel unsafe; cities can reverse the trend by creating connected safe routes and planning everyday services closer to where people live.
lessons.memory: People walk when distance feels reasonable and the route feels safe

Cause 2: unsafe streets, missing footpaths/cycle lanes and fast traffic.
Solution: connected protected networks, safer crossings and lower speeds.
Planning: place schools, shops and services within practical distance.
essay: Walking and cycling are declining as everyday travel modes in many cities. The main reasons are that common destinations are often too far apart and that streets may feel unsafe or uncomfortable for people outside vehicles. Encouraging active travel therefore requires both safer infrastructure and urban planning that makes short journeys genuinely possible.

Distance is a major barrier. When housing is separated from schools, shops and workplaces by several kilometres, walking becomes unrealistic and cycling may require considerable time. Street design can reinforce the problem. Missing footpaths, dangerous crossings, fast traffic and disconnected cycle lanes make even relatively short journeys feel risky. Parents, for example, may drive a child to a nearby school not because the distance is excessive but because the route includes a wide road with no safe crossing. Convenience then becomes linked to car use, and active travel gradually loses its normal place in daily routines.

Cities can respond by building continuous networks rather than isolated pieces of infrastructure. Protected cycle lanes should connect residential areas with stations, schools and commercial centres, while pavements need safe crossings, shade and adequate lighting. Lower vehicle speeds in neighbourhoods can further reduce perceived and actual risk. Planning policy also matters: new housing should be located near everyday services and public transport so that more journeys fall within walking or cycling distance. Secure bicycle parking at stations can extend the reach of active travel by combining it with rail or bus journeys.

In conclusion, people walk and cycle less when urban distances are long and routes are unsafe. Connected infrastructure, safer streets and more compact planning can make active travel a practical choice rather than an activity reserved for leisure.

lessons.title: Long Daily Commutes
lessons.question: Many people spend more than an hour travelling to and from work each day. Why is this happening? Is this a negative development?
lessons.thesis: Long commutes are driven by the separation between affordable housing and employment and by weak alternatives to driving; I regard the trend as negative because it consumes time and places pressure on both households and transport networks.

essay: Many workers now spend more than an hour each day travelling between home and work. This is happening mainly because affordable housing and employment are often located far apart, while transport systems do not always provide fast alternatives. I consider the trend negative because long commutes consume personal time and place additional pressure on households and urban networks.

One reason is the geography of housing and employment. Jobs may be concentrated in central business districts or specialised industrial areas, while workers move farther away to find housing they can afford. Even a moderate distance can become a long commute when roads are congested or rail connections require several transfers. In some regions, people also change jobs more frequently than they change homes, so the workplace may gradually become less convenient to reach. The result is that travel time reflects not only distance but also housing costs, job location and the quality of transport connections.

I view this as a negative development because time spent commuting has a real opportunity cost. A worker who spends two hours travelling has less time for family, exercise, rest or further study. Long journeys can also make employment less accessible to people with caring responsibilities and can concentrate demand into already crowded peak periods. Some commuting is unavoidable, and rail travel can be used productively, but this does not remove the broader cost of routinely losing large amounts of time. Cities should therefore aim to bring housing, jobs and reliable transport into better alignment.

In conclusion, long commutes are largely a result of the separation between affordable homes and employment, combined with weak or congested transport links. The trend is negative overall because it reduces personal time and increases pressure on the wider city.

This is happening because owning a vehicle is expensive and because urban residents increasingly have access to public transport, cycling and shared mobility. I regard the trend as positive where these alternatives are reliable, since people can retain mobility without bearing the financial and spatial costs of private ownership.

Cost is an important reason. Buying a car is only the beginning: drivers must also pay for insurance, fuel, maintenance and parking. For a young adult facing high housing costs, these expenses may offer poor value if the vehicle is used only occasionally. At the same time, dense cities provide alternatives that previous generations may not have had. Frequent rail services, bicycle-sharing, ride-hailing and car-sharing allow people to choose a different mode for different journeys. Digital journey-planning and payment systems have also made combining these options easier.

Overall, I see lower car ownership as positive when it reflects genuine choice rather than an inability to travel. Households can use money that would have been spent on a vehicle for housing, education or savings, while cities need less land for parking. Fewer privately owned cars may also encourage greater use of shared transport. However, the trend is not automatically beneficial in places where buses are infrequent or essential destinations are inaccessible without a car. The real objective should therefore be reliable mobility, not simply a lower ownership rate.

In conclusion, young adults are owning fewer cars because costs are high and urban alternatives have improved. This is a positive development when cities ensure that giving up ownership does not mean giving up access to work, services or social life.

lessons.title: What Makes Public Transport Attractive?
lessons.question: Cities want more people to use public transport instead of private cars. What factors are most important in making public transport attractive? Who should be responsible for improving these services?
lessons.thesis: The most important factors are reliability, useful coverage, reasonable cost and easy connections; transport authorities should set standards and coordinate networks, while operators deliver services and local governments improve street access.
lessons.memory: People switch modes when the whole journey is dependable

essay: Persuading people to use public transport requires more than purchasing new buses or trains. The most important factors are reliability, useful route coverage, reasonable fares and simple connections between services. Responsibility should be shared: public authorities need to plan and regulate the network, operators must deliver dependable services, and local governments should make stations and stops easy to reach.

Reliability is the foundation because passengers need confidence that a service will arrive and get them to their destination on time. Frequency also matters: a bus that runs every hour is difficult to use for work or appointments even if the vehicle itself is comfortable. Routes must connect the places people actually travel between, while integrated fares and clear information make transfers less stressful. Cost is important, but the cheapest service will not attract many drivers if it is slow or unpredictable. In other words, passengers judge the entire door-to-door journey rather than a single vehicle.

No single organisation can provide all these elements. Regional or city transport authorities should design the network, set service standards and coordinate fares across different operators. Bus and rail companies should be responsible for punctual operation, maintenance and staff performance. Local governments also influence the experience by providing bus lanes, safe pavements, lighting and bicycle parking around stations. Where socially necessary routes are not commercially profitable, public funding may be justified, but operators should still be monitored against clear performance targets.

In conclusion, attractive public transport depends primarily on reliability, frequency, coverage and easy connections at a reasonable price. Improvement should be a shared responsibility with clearly defined roles for authorities, operators and local governments.

lessons.title: Should Public Transport Be Free?
lessons.question: Public transport fares are a significant expense for some households. Should public transport be free for everyone? Who should pay for public transport services?
lessons.thesis: I do not support universal free fares: targeted discounts can protect people who need help while preserving revenue for service quality; funding should come from a mix of fares, public budgets and charges linked to car use where appropriate.
lessons.memory: Affordability matters, but service quality also needs stable funding

essay: Public transport fares can place pressure on low-income households, leading some people to argue that buses and trains should be free for everyone. I do not support universal free fares. Targeted discounts can protect passengers who genuinely need financial help while preserving revenue for frequent, reliable services. Public transport should therefore be funded through a combination of fares, government support and, where appropriate, charges related to car use.

Free travel has clear attractions. It removes the cost of each additional journey and may encourage some drivers to try buses or trains. However, making every journey free also gives the same subsidy to wealthy passengers who could pay. More importantly, price is only one reason people avoid public transport. A free bus that is infrequent, overcrowded or unreliable may still be unattractive. If removing fares reduces the money available for vehicles, staff or service frequency, the policy can undermine the quality that passengers depend on. I would instead offer free or reduced fares to groups for whom cost is a genuine barrier.

Funding should reflect the wider benefits that public transport creates. Passengers can reasonably contribute through fares because they receive a direct service, while governments should pay part of the cost because good transport improves access to jobs and reduces pressure on roads. Cities can also direct some parking or congestion-charge revenue towards buses and rail, linking the cost of scarce road space to better alternatives. The exact balance will differ by city, but stable funding is more important than relying on a single source.

In conclusion, public transport should be affordable but not necessarily free for everyone. Targeted fare support and a mixed funding model can protect access while maintaining the service quality required to make public transport useful.

disruption: การรบกวน/หยุดชะงัก
Construction disruption can affect shops near a new station.
ridership: ระดับ/จำนวนการใช้บริการขนส่ง
Remote work can reduce weekday transit ridership.
revenue: Fare revenue helps operators maintain frequent services.
commuting: การเดินทางไปกลับงาน/เรียน
Remote work can reduce peak-hour commuting.
adapt: Cities must adapt to changing travel patterns.
reinvest: นำกลับไปลงทุน
Cities can reinvest road-charge revenue in bus services.
mitigate: Discounts can mitigate the impact on low-income drivers.
vulnerable: เปราะบาง/ได้รับผลกระทบง่าย
Policy design should protect vulnerable users.
distributional: เกี่ยวกับการกระจายผล/ภาระระหว่างกลุ่ม
A congestion charge can have unequal distributional effects.
congestion charge: ค่าธรรมเนียมรถติด
A congestion charge can reduce peak traffic in a city centre.
high-speed rail: รถไฟความเร็วสูง
High-speed rail can compete with short-haul flights.
usually uncountable as system; a high-speed rail line
aviation: การบิน/อุตสาหกรรมการบิน
Aviation remains useful on long-distance routes.
upfront: ที่ต้องจ่าย/เกิดขึ้นตั้งแต่ต้น
High-speed rail requires substantial upfront investment.
dependence: Car dependence can limit mobility for non-drivers.
inequality: ความไม่เท่าเทียม
Weak transport can deepen inequality in access to jobs.
land-use: เกี่ยวกับการใช้ที่ดิน
Land-use planning can shorten some daily journeys.
land use เป็น noun; land-use planning ใช้ hyphen เป็น adjective
rural: Rural communities often need flexible transport services.
infrequent: ไม่บ่อย/ความถี่ต่ำ
Infrequent buses are difficult to use for appointments.
isolation: ความโดดเดี่ยว
Poor mobility can increase social isolation among older residents.
subsidy: เงินอุดหนุน
A targeted subsidy can keep an essential rural route operating.
responsive: ตอบสนองได้
Demand-responsive transport adjusts routes to bookings.
mobility: ความสามารถในการเดินทาง
Good transport protects mobility without requiring car ownership.
density: ความหนาแน่น
Low population density makes fixed routes harder to operate.
timetable: Coordinated timetables reduce waiting during transfers.
British English; schedule is common alternative
peak-hour: ช่วงเวลาเร่งด่วน
Peak-hour traffic places heavy pressure on urban roads.
peak-hour traffic/service; peak period เป็น noun phrase
coordinate: ประสานให้ทำงานร่วมกัน
Cities should coordinate transport and land-use planning.
active travel: การเดินทางที่ใช้แรงกาย
Safe streets can encourage active travel.
compact: กระชับ/ไม่กระจายตัว
Compact development can shorten everyday journeys.
commute: การเดินทางประจำไปกลับงาน/เรียน
A long commute can reduce time available for family life.
commute to work; commuting เป็น gerund/noun
affordable: ราคาจับต้องได้
Workers may live far away to find affordable housing.
affordable to/for; affordability เป็น noun
opportunity cost: ต้นทุนค่าเสียโอกาส
Long travel has an opportunity cost because it uses time that could be spent elsewhere.
economics term; explain context if used
ownership: การเป็นเจ้าของ
Car ownership is less attractive where parking is expensive.
insurance: Insurance adds to the annual cost of owning a car.
usually uncountable when referring to cover
shared mobility: บริการเดินทางแบบใช้ร่วมกัน
Shared mobility gives residents access without private ownership.
parking: การจอดรถ/พื้นที่จอด
High parking costs can discourage driving to the centre.
affordability: ความสามารถในการจ่าย
Fare affordability matters for low-income passengers.
reliability: ความน่าเชื่อถือ
Reliability is often more important than luxury features.
operator: ผู้ให้บริการ
The rail operator is responsible for day-to-day service delivery.
punctual: A punctual service builds passenger confidence.
regulate: Public authorities regulate fares and safety standards.
performance: ผลการดำเนินงาน
Operators can be monitored against performance targets.
funding: เงินทุน/การจัดสรรเงิน
Stable funding is necessary for frequent public transport.
universal: สำหรับทุกคน/ครอบคลุมทั้งหมด
Universal free fares may not be the best use of public money.
targeted: แบบเจาะจงกลุ่มเป้าหมาย
Targeted discounts can protect passengers who need support.
overcrowded: แออัดเกินไป
An overcrowded bus may discourage regular use.

asks: ตัดสินระดับความเห็นให้ชัด
ตอบ claim หลักของโจทย์โดยตรง
รักษา position เดิมตลอดทั้ง essay
Agree / Disagree.taskCorrect: Decide how far you agree or disagree and justify that position.
taskWrong: List advantages and disadvantages without taking a position.
Agree / Disagree.thinking: CLAIM → DEGREE OF AGREEMENT → REASON 1 → REASON 2 / CONCESSION → RESTATE
patterns: I largely agree/disagree that [claim] because [reason], although [concession].
ใช้บอกระดับความเห็นพร้อมยอมรับอีกด้าน
The strongest reason for my view is that [main idea].
ใช้เปิด Body ด้วย central idea ที่ชัด
Although [opposing point], this does not mean that [claim].
ใช้ concession แล้วตอบกลับโดยไม่เสีย position
patternExamples: I largely agree that cities should prioritise public transport because it moves more people efficiently, although roads still require maintenance.
The strongest reason for restricting city-centre traffic is that road space is extremely limited.
Although private cars are necessary for some journeys, this does not mean that every central street should prioritise them.

asks: อธิบายเหตุผลของทั้งสองมุมมองอย่างเป็นธรรม
ให้ความเห็นของตนเองชัดเจน
อย่าใช้ Body 1/2 เป็นเพียงการลิสต์ข้อดีข้อเสีย
Discuss Both Views + Opinion.taskCorrect: Explain both views and give a clear personal opinion.
taskWrong: Choose one view and ignore the other.
Describe only the advantages of both ideas.
Discuss Both Views + Opinion.thinking: VIEW A → WHY PEOPLE BELIEVE IT → VIEW B → WHY PEOPLE BELIEVE IT → YOUR EVALUATION
patterns: อธิบายมุมมองฝ่าย A อย่างเป็นกลาง
Those who favour [B] point out that [reason].
เปลี่ยนวิธีรายงานมุมมองอีกฝ่าย
Both positions have merit, but I believe [position] because [criterion].
ชั่งสองฝ่ายแล้วบอกความเห็น
patternExamples: Supporters of higher fuel prices argue that drivers respond to financial incentives.
Those who favour better public transport point out that behaviour changes more easily when a practical alternative exists.
Both positions have merit, but I believe better public transport should come first because it expands choice rather than merely increasing cost.

asks: ตัดสินแนวโน้มโดยรวมว่า positive หรือ negative
อธิบายผลกระทบที่สำคัญ ไม่ใช่เพียงลิสต์
ยอมรับอีกด้านได้ แต่ต้องมี overall judgement
Positive / Negative Development.taskCorrect: Judge whether the development is positive or negative overall and explain why.
taskWrong: Describe the trend without judging it.
Give equal advantages and disadvantages but no overall judgement.
Positive / Negative Development.thinking: DEVELOPMENT → MAIN BENEFIT/HARM → COUNTERPOINT → WEIGH → OVERALL JUDGEMENT
patterns: I regard this as a largely positive/negative development because [reason].
ให้ overall judgement ชัด
เปิด Body ด้วยผลกระทบหลัก
ใช้เมื่อข้อสรุปขึ้นกับเงื่อนไขจริง
patternExamples: I regard the growth of shared bicycles as a largely positive development because they can replace short car trips.
The main concern is that ride-hailing can add low-occupancy vehicles to already congested roads.
This change is positive provided that cities create safe infrastructure and clear parking rules.

asks: อธิบายข้อดีและข้อเสียให้ครบ
ไม่จำเป็นต้องเลือกผู้ชนะ เว้นแต่ต้องการสรุปเชิงสมดุล
พัฒนาแต่ละด้านด้วยกลไกและตัวอย่าง
Advantages / Disadvantages.taskCorrect: Explain meaningful advantages and disadvantages of the development.
taskWrong: Decide which side outweighs the other as the main task.
Give only your personal opinion without covering both sides.
Advantages / Disadvantages.thinking: ADVANTAGE → WHY/EXAMPLE → DISADVANTAGE → WHY/EXAMPLE → BALANCED CLOSE
patterns: เปิดข้อดีอย่างตรงประเด็น
เปิดข้อเสียด้วยคำนามที่ชัด
The value of [development] therefore depends on [condition].
สรุปแบบสมดุลโดยไม่บังคับเลือกผู้ชนะ
patternExamples: One important advantage of metro systems is that they provide high passenger capacity on busy corridors.
A significant drawback is the high upfront cost of underground construction.
The value of remote work for transport therefore depends on how cities adapt services to changing demand.

asks: อธิบายทั้งข้อดีและข้อเสีย
ตัดสินว่าด้านใดมีน้ำหนักมากกว่า
ชั่งตามขนาด ระยะเวลา กลุ่มคน หรือความแก้ไขได้ ไม่ใช่นับจำนวนข้อ
Do Advantages Outweigh Disadvantages?.taskCorrect: Discuss both sides and decide which carries greater weight.
taskWrong: List two advantages and one disadvantage and assume the advantages win.
Describe both sides without making a comparison.
Do Advantages Outweigh Disadvantages?.thinking: WEAKER SIDE → STRONGER SIDE → COMPARISON CRITERION → VERDICT
patterns: Although [drawback] is significant, [benefit] carries greater weight because [comparison].
ชั่งน้ำหนักโดยมีเกณฑ์
เทียบด้านด้วยระยะเวลา/ผลกระทบ
The advantages outweigh the disadvantages when [condition].
สรุป verdict แบบมีเงื่อนไข
patternExamples: Although congestion charges can burden some drivers, reduced traffic carries greater weight because the benefits extend across the network.
Unlike a temporary construction cost, a well-used rail line can provide capacity for decades.
The advantages of high-speed rail outweigh the disadvantages when passenger demand is consistently strong.

asks: ระบุผลเสีย/ปัญหาที่เกิดจากสถานการณ์
เสนอทางแก้ที่จับคู่กับปัญหา
อธิบายว่าใครทำอะไรและทำไมจึงช่วยได้
Problems + Solutions.taskCorrect: Explain the problems caused and propose measures that address them.
taskWrong: Explain only why the situation happens.
List solutions without showing which problem they solve.
Problems + Solutions.thinking: PROBLEM → CONSEQUENCE → MATCHING SOLUTION → ACTOR + ACTION + MECHANISM
patterns: ระบุปัญหาหลักอย่างชัด
จับคู่ปัญหากับผู้ลงมือแก้
อธิบายกลไกของทางแก้
patternExamples: One major problem is that car dependence can restrict access for people who cannot drive.
To address this problem, governments should provide reliable alternatives to private cars.
This would help by allowing households to reach jobs and services without owning a vehicle.

asks: อธิบายสาเหตุของแนวโน้มหรือปัญหา
แยก cause ออกจาก symptom
เสนอวิธีที่แก้ต้นเหตุหรือแรงจูงใจนั้นจริง
Causes + Solutions.taskCorrect: Explain the main causes and propose measures that target those causes.
taskWrong: Describe only the problems created by the trend.
Suggest general solutions without identifying why the trend occurs.
Causes + Solutions.thinking: CAUSE 1/2 → WHY THEY OPERATE → TARGETED MEASURE → HOW IT CHANGES THE CAUSE
patterns: ระบุสาเหตุ ไม่ใช่ผลกระทบ
เพิ่มปัจจัยที่ทำให้สาเหตุแรงขึ้น
[Actor] can reduce this problem by [targeted action].
เชื่อม solution กับ mechanism
patternExamples: One important cause is that new road capacity can encourage additional car use.
This pressure can be reinforced by housing located far from employment centres.
Cities can reduce this problem by coordinating land use with high-quality public transport.

asks: นับคำถามย่อยให้ครบ
ตอบคำถามแรกและคำถามที่สองอย่างสมดุล
Conclusion ต้องสรุปคำตอบทั้งสอง ไม่ใช่เพียงส่วนเดียว
Two-Part Question.taskCorrect: Answer both explicit questions directly and develop each answer.
taskWrong: Answer only the first question in detail.
Treat the prompt as a generic advantages/disadvantages essay.
Two-Part Question.thinking: QUESTION 1 → DIRECT ANSWER + WHY → QUESTION 2 → DIRECT JUDGEMENT + WHY
patterns: ตอบ why ตรง ๆ
I consider this a positive/negative development because [reason].
ตอบ judgement ตรง ๆ
สรุปสองคำตอบในประโยคเดียว
patternExamples: This is happening mainly because affordable housing is often located far from major employment centres.
I consider this a negative development because long commutes consume time that could be used for family or rest.
Overall, commuting is lengthening because homes and jobs are separated, while the trend is negative because it reduces personal time.

asks: แยกคำถามย่อยทุกข้อ
ตอบตรง ไม่ต้องบังคับเข้าหมวดสำเร็จรูป
จัด Body ตามคำถามหรือกลุ่มคำตอบที่ชัดที่สุด
Direct Question.taskCorrect: Answer each direct question explicitly and support the answers.
taskWrong: Discuss the topic generally without answering every question.
Force the response into an agree/disagree structure.
Direct Question.thinking: QUESTION 1 → DIRECT ANSWER → QUESTION 2 → DIRECT ANSWER → SUPPORT BOTH
patterns: The most important [skills/factors] are [A, B and C] because [reason].
ตอบ direct question ด้วยขอบเขตชัด
แบ่งความรับผิดชอบระหว่างสองฝ่าย
A shared approach is preferable because [reason].
สรุปเมื่อคำตอบต้องแบ่งบทบาท
patternExamples: The most important service factors are reliability, frequency and route coverage because passengers need a dependable door-to-door journey.
Transport authorities should coordinate the network, while operators should deliver punctual services.
A shared funding approach is preferable because passengers and the wider public both benefit from effective transport.

Agree / Disagree: ยอมรับข้อโต้แย้งโดยยังรักษาจุดยืน เช่น Although X is valuable, Y remains necessary.
เพิ่มรายละเอียดโดยไม่แยกเป็นประโยคสั้นหลายประโยค เช่น commuters who lack a reliable alternative.
อธิบายผลที่อาจเกิดขึ้น เช่น If public transport is reliable, some drivers will change modes.
ใช้ this view / this policy / these measures เพื่อลดการพูดซ้ำและเพิ่ม cohesion.
Discuss Both Views + Opinion: วางสองมุมมองให้เห็นความต่างอย่างเป็นธรรมชาติ.
ใช้ supporters argue that / those who favour... เพื่อรายงานความเห็นโดยไม่ทำให้เป็นความเห็นของผู้เขียน.
ขยายกลุ่มคนหรือแนวคิด เช่น commuters whose areas lack rail services.
ใช้ but / even though เพื่อบอกความเห็นของผู้เขียนหลังอธิบายทั้งสองฝ่าย.
Positive / Negative Development: ใส่เงื่อนไขเมื่อการตัดสินเชิงบวกหรือลบขึ้นกับวิธีดำเนินการ.
ขยายกลุ่มที่ได้รับผล เช่น passengers who depend on late-night transport.
เชื่อมกลไก เช่น so / therefore / which can...
ย่อความสัมพันธ์ของการกระทำ เช่น reducing barriers / allowing learners to...
Advantages / Disadvantages: เปลี่ยนจากข้อดีไปข้อเสียโดยไม่ใช้ connector ซ้ำมากเกินไป.
อธิบายกลุ่มหรือระบบ เช่น routes that serve low-density areas.
ใช้ can / may เพื่อหลีกเลี่ยงการเหมารวมผลกระทบ.
เปรียบเทียบค่าใช้จ่ายหรือประสิทธิภาพ เช่น more expensive than / more practical than.
Do Advantages Outweigh Disadvantages?: ใช้ greater / broader / more significant เพื่อชั่งน้ำหนัก ไม่ใช่แค่ลิสต์.
ยอมรับด้านที่อ่อนกว่าแล้วกลับไป verdict.
เพิ่มรายละเอียดของกลุ่มผู้ใช้ เส้นทาง หรือข้อจำกัดโดยไม่แตกเป็นหลายประโยค.
ใช้ when / if เพื่อกำหนดเงื่อนไขที่ verdict เป็นจริง.
Problems + Solutions: แสดงว่าปัญหานำไปสู่อะไร เช่น can lead to / result in.
ใช้ should / can / could เพื่อเสนอทางแก้อย่างเหมาะสม.
ใช้ to address / to reduce เพื่อเชื่อม action กับ purpose.
ขยายกลุ่มคนหรือระบบที่ได้รับผล เช่น residents who cannot drive.
Causes + Solutions: ใช้ is caused by / is driven by / because เพื่อแยกสาเหตุจากผล.
เหมาะเมื่อผู้กระทำไม่สำคัญ เช่น road space is often treated as unlimited.
ใช้ by providing / by improving เพื่ออธิบายกลไกของทางแก้.
แสดงผลของมาตรการ เช่น students are more likely to choose science if...
Two-Part Question: ตอบ Why ด้วยสาเหตุที่ชัด ไม่วนเกริ่น.
ขยายกลุ่มคนหรือสถานการณ์โดยไม่เพิ่มประโยคแยก.
ยอมรับข้อจำกัดก่อน overall judgement.
ทำให้ผู้อ่านเห็นชัดว่า Body 1 ตอบ Q1 และ Body 2 ตอบ Q2.
Direct Question: ใช้รูปแบบคู่ขนานเมื่อแจกแจงทักษะหรือบทบาทหลายฝ่าย.
ใช้ should เพื่อเสนอความรับผิดชอบหรือแนวนโยบาย.
ขยายผู้โดยสาร เส้นทาง หรือบริการโดยไม่ทำให้ประโยคแตก.
เช่น targeted fare support / integrated transport network ช่วยเขียนกระชับและเป็นวิชาการ.

Agree / Disagree: I am agree with this statement.
agree เป็น verb จึงไม่ใช้ am agree
I agree with to this idea.
agree with + noun; agree to ใช้กับ proposal/terms บางบริบท ไม่ใช้ with to
From my opinion, public transport should...
In my opinion, public transport should...
fixed phrase ที่เป็นธรรมชาติคือ In my opinion / In my view / From my perspective
Discuss Both Views + Opinion: I will discuss about both views.
discuss เป็น transitive verb ไม่ต้องมี about
There are two views and I will discuss them.
Both views have merit, but I favour...
ประโยคแรกไม่ผิดไวยากรณ์ แต่ยังไม่ให้ own opinion ตามโจทย์
Positive / Negative Development: This is positive and negative development.
This is a largely positive development.
ต้องมี article และควรให้ overall judgement
It depends of how cities manage it.
It depends on how cities manage it.
depend on เป็น collocation
Advantages / Disadvantages: One of the advantage is flexibility.
One of the advantages is flexibility.
ใช้ there are ไม่ใช่ there have
offer/provide convenience เป็น collocation ที่เป็นธรรมชาติกว่า
Do Advantages Outweigh Disadvantages?: The advantages outweigh than the disadvantages.
outweigh + object โดยตรง ไม่มี than
There are more advantages, so they outweigh.
The advantages carry greater weight because...
ต้องชั่ง impact ไม่ใช่นับจำนวนข้อ
Although it is expensive, but it is useful.
Although it is expensive, it is useful.
ไม่ใช้ although และ but เชื่อม clause เดียวกันซ้ำ
Problems + Solutions: This problem can cause to stress.
cause + noun; หรือ cause someone to + verb
The government should improve bus services.
modal + base verb ไม่มี to; ใช้ the government เมื่อหมายถึงรัฐบาลหนึ่ง
Cities should solve this issue by awareness.
Cities should address this issue by improving alternatives.
by + gerund/action; awareness อย่างเดียวไม่บอกกลไก
Causes + Solutions: The reason is because people drive more.
One reason is that people drive more.
reason is that เป็นรูปมาตรฐานกว่า reason is because
lack เป็น verb ได้: lack + noun; หรือ have a lack of
By improve buses, cities can help.
By improving bus services, cities can help.
Two-Part Question: The reason why is because housing is far away.
This is mainly because housing is far from jobs.
หลีกเลี่ยง reason why is because ที่ซ้ำความหมาย
This trend is positive / a positive development.
positive เป็น adjective; ถ้าใช้ article ต้องตามด้วย noun
I will answer both questions in this essay.
Adults return to education because..., and I see this as positive because...
ไม่จำเป็นต้องประกาศโครง essay; ใช้พื้นที่ตอบคำถามโดยตรง
Direct Question: Cities should provide people about better buses.
Cities should provide people with better bus services.
provide someone with something / provide something for someone
The government should set transport policy and service standards.
government มักต้องมี the เมื่อหมายถึงรัฐบาลหนึ่ง และควรใช้ verb ให้ตรงหน้าที่
